title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
corePattern: Binary Search on Partition Index over Smaller Array
interviewTips: Ask if either array can be empty and confirm total length can be 1, and whether integers can be negative or duplicates.
Trade-off: O(m+n) merge is simplest and least bug-prone, while O(log(min(m,n))) binary-search partition is expected for Hard with O(1) space.
Edge-case tip: handle odd vs even total length separately and use -inf/inf sentinels for empty partition sides to avoid index checks.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Merge and Sort
approaches.intuition: If we put all elements together and sort them, the median is just the middle element or average of two middles. Correctness is obvious and easy to code first.
approaches.theory: Concatenate both arrays into one array of size m+n, sort it, then pick index n//2 for odd length or average of n//2-1 and n//2 for even length. Sorting guarantees order, so median definition applies directly.

timeComplexity.explanation: Concatenation is O(m+n) and sorting the combined array dominates with O((m+n) log(m+n)).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Extra merged array stores all m+n elements.

edgeCases: Duplicates and negatives work because sort handles them

approaches.name: Approach 2: Linear Merge with Two Pointers
approaches.intuition: Since inputs are already sorted, we can merge like in merge-sort and stop when we reach the median position, without storing everything.
approaches.theory: Let total=m+n, mid1=(total-1)//2 and mid2=total//2 (same for odd, two middles for even). Walk with i,j pointers picking smaller head each step, counting steps. Record values at mid1 and mid2, then average. This simulates merge order in O(m+n) steps.

timeComplexity.explanation: In worst case we advance pointers up to median position, at most O((m+n)/2 +1) steps, bounded by O(m+n).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only a few indices and two median candidates are stored.

edgeCases: One array empty: nums1=[], nums2=[2,3] -> walk only second array
Even total: nums1=[1,2], nums2=[3,4] -> mid1=1,mid2=2, a=2,b=3 -> 2.5
All elements in one array smaller than other

approaches.name: Approach 3: Optimal Binary Search Partition
approaches.intuition: Median splits the combined sorted array into left half and right half with all left <= all right. If we cut the small array at i and the large array at j so left sizes sum to half, we only need to find the correct cut with binary search.
approaches.theory: Ensure nums1 is smaller. Let half=(m+n+1)//2. For partition i in [0..m], j=half-i. Define Aleft,Aright,Bleft,Bright with -inf/inf for out-of-bounds. Correct partition satisfies Aleft<=Bright and Bleft<=Aright. Then odd median is max(Aleft,Bleft), even is (max left + min right)/2. The condition is monotonic in i, so binary search on i finds it in O(log(min(m,n))).

timeComplexity.explanation: Binary search runs over the smaller array of length min(m,n), each step O(1).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only partition indices and four border values are used.

steps: Ensure nums1 smaller? swap -> nums1=[2], nums2=[1,3], m=1,n=2,half=2

edgeCases: Empty small array: nums1=[], nums2=[1,2,3] -> i=0 fixed, j=half
Even total: nums1=[1,2], nums2=[3,4] -> half=2, partition found, (2+3)/2=2.5
Large skew: m=1,n=100000, binary search stays logarithmic
